title: POC scoping - Equinox Data (Latency SLOs)

Agreed measurement definitions for TTFT and TPOT, p95/p99 targets tentatively set, workload sizing (QPS and concurrency), and a benchmark plan using replay + synthetic load. Next steps: Redwood to send benchmark harness and pricing for Dedicated vs Hosted, customer to share sample prompt corpus and production traffic patterns.

transcript:
Header:
Date: 2027-08-03 15:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Jonas Rivera (Redwood SE), Ari Chen (Redwood SA), Samir Gupta (Equinox CTO), Lena Morales (Lead ML Eng), Tariq Ahmed (SRE), Priya Rao (PM)

SUMMARY BLOCK (auto):
- Focus: define TTFT vs TPOT, p95/p99 targets, workload sizing and measurement plan for a 2-week POC.
- Agreed on measurement harness (replay + synthetic), acceptance criteria and next steps.

Transcript: (timestamps approximate, auto captions sometimes off)
00:00 Maya: hey everyone, thanks for taking the time. um we'll run through scope for the poc focusing on latency SLOs and measurement plan, jonas will cover the benchmarking approach.
00:12 Samir: yeah thanks, quick context — Equinox runs an internal assistant and document QA pipelines, peak is roughly 80 QPS across clusters but 24-hour avg is 12 QPS, lots of medium-length prompts. We're most sensitive to first token latency for the interactive assistant.
00:24 Jonas: great, thanks. quick clarifying q: when you say "first token" you mean time-to-first-token TTFT measured at the edge or at the model container?
00:31 Lena: at the user-facing edge — perceived by end users so network + routing included but we'd like Redwood to separate out model-infer times for root-cause.
00:40 Ari: yeah we usually report both: TTFT (client send -> first byte returned) and TPOT which we use internally for per-token tail behavior (time-per-token). we'll also capture GPU kernel latencies and batch sizes so you can see batching effects.
00:53 Tariq: ok that makes sense. what targets should we be aiming for? p95 and p99?
01:00 Jonas: rough ballpark — for an assistant use-case with ~120 token outputs we usually aim for TTFT p95 <= 220ms and p99 <= 420ms on a dedicated low-latency config; TPOT p95 <= 16ms/token and p99 <= 35ms/token, that aligns with what we've seen on Redwood-verified models.
01:15 Samir: those numbers look promising but can you explain TPOT in practice? i'm worried per-token adds up for longer responses.
01:22 Maya: sure, TPOT is the per-token generation time once the model has started streaming; multiply TPOT by number of tokens to estimate streaming wall time minus overlapping network send. TTFT matters for perceived responsiveness — the first token is the big UX win.
01:36 Lena: our median response length is ~110 tokens, 90th is 220. our interactive flows also have short replies (10-30 tokens) where TTFT dominates perception.
01:45 Jonas: important for benchmark design — we'll run two workload shapes: conversational interactive (short replies, high TTFT sensitivity) and long-form generation (long responses, TPOT sensitivity). we'll also test mixed traffic to reproduce real distribution.
01:58 Priya: timeline? how long for the POC?
02:02 Maya: typical is 2 weeks of hands-on benchmarking: one week for setup + tuning and one week of steady-state runs and regression tests. given you want SLO verification we'll do baseline runs, then spike tests, and then kernel-level profiling if tails are bad.
02:15 Samir: sounds good. can you talk about measurement specifics — p95/p99 definitions and what we actually measure?
02:22 Jonas: yes. measurement plan notes — this will be in the harness doc but verbally:
- TTFT: measured at ingress LB (timestamp when request received) to the time first byte leaves Redwood inference service. we'll record both client-observed TTFT and service-side TTFT (so network removed).
- TPOT: measured service-side as average delta between token k and k+1 once generation begins; we capture per-token latencies and compute p50/p95/p99. TPOT excludes initial decode/compilation jitter.
02:50 Maya: we'll export these metrics to Prometheus and create Grafana dashboards — we will also produce a CSV of per-request traces for offline analysis.
02:58 Tariq: for load profile, what's the QPS/concurrency plan?
03:02 Jonas: propose these preliminary sizing targets for POC:
- Steady-state: 50 QPS (matches your 24h avg headroom for safe testing)
- Peak spike: 200 QPS sustained for 10 minutes to test autoscaling and tail behavior
- Concurrency: simulate 300 concurrent connections with typical think times to approximate user behavior
- Payloads: 500 sample prompts reflecting your short/long distribution (Lena to provide)
03:30 Samir: is 50 QPS realistic? earlier we said 80 QPS peak — we intend to test both avg and peak, ok.
03:36 Jonas: yes we'll do both — steady 50 and a stress run at 80 and 200. also we'll vary batch sizes: no batching (single-token) and smart batching (up to 8) to see cost/latency tradeoffs.
03:50 Lena: do you support KV cache/prefix cache? we heavily use system-level prefixes for context.
03:55 Ari: yes, Redwood runtime supports KV cache and prefix caching. for POC we'll test with cache cold and warm conditions and report cache hit rates — caches materially shift TTFT.
04:06 Samir: ok, acceptance criteria? we need explicit pass/fail for the POC.
04:10 Maya: propose acceptance criteria (we can tweak):
- For interactive flows (short replies): TTFT p95 <= 250ms and p99 <= 450ms when cache warm, or documented explanation if not met with mitigation plan.
- For long-form workloads: TPOT p95 <= 18ms/token and p99 <= 40ms/token and end-to-end median throughput >= 40 QPS for the target instance config.
- Stability: no more than 2% error rate and no OOMs or node restarts during steady-state 1-hour runs.
04:40 Samir: that seems reasonable, i want p95 tighter on TTFT if possible but let's start with your numbers and iterate.
04:47 Jonas: we'll also capture system-level signals: GPU util, batch sizes, kernel time, network egress, and queue lengths so we can propose tuning knobs (smaller batch size for latency, quantization options for cost).
04:58 Priya: what's the difference in cost between Hosted and Dedicated for this POC?
05:02 Maya: i'll send a side-by-side — Hosted quickstart is faster but may have multi-tenant variability; Dedicated gives predictable tails and isolation. for a strict p99 target we usually recommend Dedicated POC if you're measuring deep tail behavior.
05:17 Tariq: security question — we need SOC2, SSO, and KMS integration for private keys?
05:22 Maya: Redwood supports SAML/SSO, SOC2 attestation, and KMS integration for private deployments. for Dedicated we can provide private VPC peering and dedicated GPUs. we'll attach Security pack docs in the follow-up.
05:34 Samir: ok perfect. anything else on measurement?
05:38 Jonas: one more thing: for p99 we recommend long-duration tail tests (at least 1 hour steady with sampling), and a separate kernel-profiling run where we capture per-layer times to see if attention kernels or KV cache are main contributors.
05:52 Lena: good. how will you handle variability from our side (network jitter, proxies)?
05:57 Ari: we'll instrument both client-side and service-side timestamps and correlate. we'll also replay production requests in a controlled env to minimize external noise, then run open-network runs to validate user-perceived TTFT.
06:08 Maya: ok final recap — deliverables: benchmark harness + scripts, dashboard templates, pricing and infra proposal, POC schedule. customer provides prompts and logs. we'll run 2-week POC with the tests described.
06:22 Samir: thanks all, i think we have a clear plan.
06:25 Maya: thanks. i'll follow up with the harness link and calendar invite for the hands-on run. bye all.

Notes and minor transcription quirks: speaker turns sometimes merged, a few product names were auto captioned ("Redwood Dedicate" -> "Redwood Dedicated"), timestamps approximate.
